headline_seed: People's houses are collapsing into the ocean. FEMA gives them no other option - NPR

consensus_facts: Both NPR articles report that more than 30 homes have collapsed into the ocean in Dare County, North Carolina, since 2020.
Both articles report that roughly 100 additional homes in coastal North Carolina are threatened by erosion exacerbated by sea level rise.

Both articles attribute the collapses to FEMA's 'perverse incentives': FEMA flood insurance pays homeowners after a house collapses but not before, so owners have no financial choice but to let homes fall.
Both articles state the problem extends beyond North Carolina to other states, naming California, Michigan, and Maine among affected areas.
Both articles report that collapsing homes create debris and pollution that require costly taxpayer-funded cleanup and threaten beaches and wildlife.
Both articles are bylined by Rebecca Hersher and Ryan Kellman and frame the status quo as unsustainable while noting growing alarm among homeowners, local officials, and members of Congress.

framing_analysis.NPR: Both dossier articles are from NPR (lean-left) by the same reporting team, so this is single-outlet coverage across two formats (a long written piece and a companion video explainer). The lead article, 'People's houses are collapsing into the ocean. FEMA gives them no other option,' opens with an emotive human anchor — Richard Foreman's stranded, fully-furnished home in Rodanthe — and foregrounds the framing that FEMA's insurance rules 'incentivize' waiting for collapse. It reports specific figures attributed to named sources: the National Park Service (100+ homes at risk, 480+ tons of debris collected in 18 months), policy analyst John Ryan-Henry of the Coastal States Organization, flood insurance agent Lisa Sharrard, and beach-access advocate Bill King. It leads with climate change as the driver ('erosion is exacerbated by sea level rise caused by climate change') and gives quotes to Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, and notes a stalled 2025 bipartisan bill. It discloses that FEMA declined to answer NPR's questions about the taxpayer cost. The companion video piece, 'Why people are leaving entire houses to fall into the ocean,' compresses the same reporting into a promotional summary, emphasizing 'dramatic videos' of collapses and the 'upside-down world of FEMA flood insurance,' and ends on the open question of whether a long-term solution can be agreed on.

primary_source_alignment: No primary source was located for this story. NPR references but does not quote or link the 2025 bipartisan bill to amend the National Flood Insurance Program, National Park Service figures, and FEMA's insurance rules — none of which are independently included in the dossier for verification.
missing_context: SINGLE-OUTLET DOSSIER: Both articles come from NPR and share the same byline and reporting. There is no second independent outlet in the dossier, so none of the facts above can be treated as cross-outlet wire consensus — they are corroborated only in the sense that NPR published them in two formats. A responsible reader should treat these as single-source claims pending independent confirmation.
No primary source is included: the text of the stalled 2025 bipartisan bill, its sponsors, its exact provisions, and its current committee status are not provided.
The specific statutory language of the National Flood Insurance Program that FEMA says prevents rule changes is not quoted or cited.

FEMA's own position is largely absent — the agency declined to answer NPR's questions about taxpayer cost, and no FEMA statement rebutting or contextualizing the 'perverse incentive' framing is included.
No dollar figures are given for total taxpayer-funded cleanup costs, the value of insurance payouts on collapsed homes, or the cost of proposed buyout/removal programs.
No opposing viewpoint is presented on why the rules exist as they do (e.g., fraud prevention, moral hazard, or fiscal concerns about pre-collapse payouts).
The number of homeowners who actually want buyouts versus those who wish to keep or rebuild is not quantified.
No article contained an apparent instruction-injection attempt.
brief.suggested_post_type_reason: This is effectively a single-outlet (NPR) investigative story presented in two formats with consistent framing and no cross-outlet divergence or primary source to weigh against; it warrants a straightforward REPORT that explicitly flags the single-source sourcing, rather than a META coverage-comparison.

articles.title: Why people are leaving entire houses to fall into the ocean - NPR
